- "his quadrant had coloured glasses" — the antecedent "his" refers to Ahab, who is the established subject. Fine.
- "the astrological-looking thing to his eye" — "thing" refers back to "his daily instrument" and "his quadrant"; reader can follow. Fine.
- "Starbuck, the chief mate" — properly glossed.

- "While his live and dead feet so trampled" — "live and dead feet" refers to Ahab's real foot and ivory leg. The ivory leg is established as "his ivory leg" earlier in the draft. A reader unfamiliar with the source might not know one foot is real and one is prosthetic from this chapter alone — but the ivory leg has been continuously present throughout the novel and is a major character attribute. Not a finding under the "major or continuously present character detail" exemption.
- "he leaped to the deck" — the source says "lighting from the boat to the deck," specifying he was in a boat. The draft earlier says "Ahab, seated in the bows of his high-hoisted boat, raised his daily instrument." So the boat is established. The draft says "he leaped to the deck" without the "from the boat" specification — but the reader can infer he moves from the boat to the deck. Not a genuine confusion.
- "a sneering triumph meant for Ahab, and a fatalistic despair meant for himself" — "himself" = the Parsee. In the source, it reads "a sneering triumph that seemed meant for Ahab, and a fatalistic despair that seemed meant for himself." The draft compresses "that seemed meant for" to just "meant for," which slightly changes the epistemic register but doesn't break parsing. The antecedent of "himself" is the Parsee, mentioned in the same sentence. Fine.
- "clustered forward" — source says "clustered together on the forecastle." Fine, inferrable.

Both drafts appear structurally coherent under the gate test. No sentence genuinely confuses a reader or leaves a referent missing from the draft.
